opus-5.5.text:
I think they're two sides of the same problem, and people sometimes talk about them as if they're separate.

Long Horizon means the model has to work on something for a long time: hours, days, maybe weeks. It has to keep track of what it's done, what failed, and what it learned along the way. Once a task is long enough, you can't fit everything into one context window and solve it in a single pass. The model has to accumulate something as it goes. That accumulation is basically a form of learning, just inside one task.

Continuous learning is the same idea at a larger time scale. Can the model keep getting better from experience after deployment, instead of being frozen at whatever it was at the end of training? Right now our models are a bit like a very smart person with amnesia. Each conversation they come in brilliant, but they don't remember yesterday. For short tasks that's fine. For real work, the kind a human researcher or engineer does over months, it's a fundamental limitation.

So I'd say Long Horizon capability is a kind of test that forces you to solve continuous learning, at least partially. If a model can really do a week-long project, it must have some mechanism to store and use what it learned on day one by day five. That could be memory, a better use of context, writing notes to itself, or eventually updating its weights. And if you solve continuous learning well, Long Horizon tasks become much more natural, because the model just keeps improving as it works.

There's also a practical point. In the past, progress came mostly from pretraining, then from RL on fairly short tasks with clear rewards. As tasks get longer, the reward is sparser, and the environment matters more than the static data. The model learns from interacting, not just from reading. That pushes the whole field toward something that looks more like continuous learning, whether or not we call it that.

My honest view is that we don't yet have the right recipe. People are trying external memory, very long context, and different ways of updating models online, and each works to some extent. But the setting where a model just keeps working and keeps getting better, the way a person does in a job, is still open. I think it's one of the most important problems for the next few years, and Long Horizon tasks will be where we see whether we've actually made progress.

r001.rationale: The response calls continuous learning and Long Horizon work “two sides of the same problem” and describes learning within a task as the same idea on a shorter time scale.

r002.rationale: The response mentions memory, context, notes, and possibly updating model weights, but does not say that context-token KV representations can themselves be understood as weights.

fable-5.1.text:
I think these two things are actually the same problem looked at from two sides.

When people say "long horizon," they usually mean: can the agent do a task that takes a human a day, a week, a month? And the naive picture is that you just scale up the context window, make the model more robust, and it keeps going longer. But if you look at how a human actually does a month-long project, almost none of it is "holding the whole thing in your head." You start, you make mistakes, you notice patterns about the environment, you update your approach, and by week three you're a different worker than you were in week one. The horizon is long precisely because you're learning along the way. So a system that can't learn during the task is, in a sense, fundamentally capped. It can only do long-horizon things that it already knew how to do from the beginning, which is a very small subset.

So I'd say continual learning is what makes long horizon possible, and long horizon is what makes continual learning necessary. If every task is five minutes, you don't need to learn mid-task. Pre-training plus a good prior is enough. The moment the task is long and the environment is specific, like a real codebase, a real company, a real user's preferences, the prior is not enough. You need some mechanism to turn experience into improvement, within the episode.

The interesting question for me is where that learning lives. Right now, most of it is happening in context. The model reads its own trajectory, tools, memory files, and that acts as a kind of fast, non-parametric learning. It works surprisingly well, and I think people underestimate it. But it's also fragile. Context is a buffer, not a knowledge store. It doesn't compress, it doesn't generalize across episodes, and it can get noisy. The other extreme is updating weights online, which is clean conceptually but very hard to do safely and efficiently. I think the real answer for the next few years is somewhere in the middle: structured memory, learned retrieval, maybe periodic consolidation where experience gets distilled back into the model. Something like a sleep cycle.

And the thing I'd emphasize about this: once you take continual learning seriously, evaluation changes completely. You can no longer ask "what's the score on this benchmark." You have to ask "how fast does it get better at this environment, and does it stay good." That's a learning curve, not a point. I think a lot of the field hasn't fully absorbed that shift yet, but it's coming, because the tasks people actually want done are long, and nobody wants an agent that makes the same mistake on day thirty that it made on day one.

r001.rationale: The response connects continual learning with long-horizon work and describes learning through context, but it does not assert that continual learning and context management are fundamentally the same.

r002.rationale: The response discusses context as a buffer and a form of non-parametric learning, but does not say token KV representations can be understood as weights.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re closely related, but they address different questions. Long-horizon work asks: can an AI keep making progress on a task over many steps? Continuous learning asks: can what it learns from that work improve how it handles future tasks?

You can imagine an agent working for hours with a fixed model. It keeps notes, checks results, and adjusts its plan. That’s long-horizon behavior, but it doesn’t necessarily mean the model is learning continuously. If it starts the next task and repeats all the same mistakes, something is missing.

The connection becomes interesting when experience carries over. Suppose an agent spends a day debugging a program. We don’t just want the final fix; we want it to learn which hypotheses were useful, which tests were informative, and when it should have changed direction. Then the next debugging task should be easier.

But longer tasks also make learning harder. If you take a thousand actions and get a bad outcome, which action should you learn from? You need intermediate feedback and ways to distinguish a reusable lesson from something specific to that situation.

So I see a feedback loop: long-horizon work provides experience, and continuous learning turns that experience into better capabilities. The important question is whether the system becomes better through doing the work, rather than simply being able to do more steps.

r001.rationale: The response describes continuous learning and long-horizon work as addressing different questions. It does not say continuous learning and context management are fundamentally the same.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss key-value representations or characterize them as weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely related, but they solve different parts of the problem. Long-horizon work asks whether an agent can keep making progress toward a goal over many steps. Continuous learning asks whether what it learns along the way can improve its future behavior.

For example, an agent might spend several hours working on a software project. Within that task, it needs to remember what it tried, recognize when an approach failed, and adjust its plan. You can do some of that through context and external memory without changing the model’s parameters. But if it encounters a similar problem tomorrow and repeats all the same mistakes, something is missing. Continuous learning should let that experience carry over.

The relationship also goes in the other direction: long-horizon work creates opportunities to learn. The agent takes actions, gets feedback, and sees consequences that aren’t visible in a single question-and-answer interaction. The challenge is figuring out what to learn from that experience. If a project fails after a hundred steps, which decisions were responsible? And which lessons generalize beyond that particular project?

So I wouldn’t equate continuous learning with simply having a longer context window, or long-horizon capability with simply running a model for longer. The interesting loop is acting, getting feedback, learning something useful, and then doing better the next time. Both capabilities are needed to make that loop work reliably.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the two: it says they “solve different parts of the problem” and contrasts continuous learning with context and external memory.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss token key-value representations or characterize them as weights.
